+basal areas, and were poorly rooted compared to Themeda tussocks in a frequently burnt area. Litter levels were also much greater in the undisturbed area and covered all the intertussock spaces. McDougall (1989) concluded that without ®re or grazing, ``long unburnt Themeda tussocks could be expected to disappear from the sward'' and seedling recruitment would be minimal under the dead thatch. In the following 10 yr, Themeda health declined further as a result of continued ®re exclusion, leading to the death of many tussocks (Lunt and Morgan, 1998).

+At the Derrimut Grassland Reserve in southern Victoria, Australia, ®re is considered a necessary conservation management tool to maintain native species diversity (Craigie and Stuwe, 1992), but it has been applied in an adhoc manner since the creation of the reserve in 1985. Some areas have been burnt three times over the last 12 yr (maximum inter-®re interval of 4 yr), whilst other areas have never been burnt. Lunt and Morgan (1999) reported on the ¯oristic changes that occurred during the ®rst 10 yr of reservation and found that most native species that had survived long-term grazing were also fairly resilient to the variable ®re regimes imposed. Surprisingly, the least resilient species to infrequent burning and grazing exclusion appeared to be the dominant tussock grass, Themeda triandra. This ®nding has important implications for the threatened fauna that rely on the grassland for habitat (e.g. the Striped Legless Lizard, Delma impar), as well as the susceptibility of the grassland community to invasion by exotic perennial grasses (Lunt and Morgan, submitted). In this paper, we investigate how timesince-®re aects the survival, vigour, structure and productivity of Themeda triandra tussocks, and the subsequent ability of tussocks to recover from ®re.
+### 2. Methods
+# 2.1. Study site

+The 154 ha Derrimut Grassland Reserve is 15 km south-west of Melbourne, Victoria (37480 3000S, 144470 4000E). Mean annual rainfall is 568 mm. The geology is Early Pleistocene olivine basalt (Douglas, 1982). The reserve is dominated by a Themeda triandra grassland in well-drained areas (Lunt, 1990a) and is a remnant of the Keilor Plains grassland described by Willis (1964). This grassland type is on the verge of extinction (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994). Soils in grassland areas range from silty-clay to clay-loam with pH 7.0 (Lunt, 1990a).

+The property was grazed by sheep until the 1960s and by cattle from then until 1985, when grazing was removed from the entire site after management changed to the state conservation agency for the purposes of grassland conservation.

+Early recommendations for management of the reserve suggested that ®re at 2±5 yr intervals were necessary to maintain botanical values (Stuwe, 1986; Lunt, 1988). However, owing to perceived negative impacts of frequent burning on endangered fauna (Coulson, 1990), a management plan recommended that the reserve be divided into 10 zones, two of which were to be burnt every year, giving a 5 yr ®re interval in each zone (Craigie and Stuwe, 1992). In practice, the management plan has not been consistently implemented. Ten ®res occurred between 1986 and 1997 but all had dierent boundaries and burnt dierent areas. The number of ®res experienced in each zone ranged from 0 to 3 and the maximum inter-®re interval varied from 4 to over 12 yr (in areas which were never burnt).
+# 2.2. Study species

+Themeda triandra (syn. T. australis) is a perennial C4 tussock grass that dominates many grassy woodlands and tropical savannahs in both Australia and Africa. In southern Victoria, T. triandra is the dominant species of natural grassland communities on volcanic soils (Patton, 1935; Willis, 1964; McDougall et al., 1994). It grows primarily from October to January in southern Victoria and is most productive in the ®rst 3±4 yr after ®re (McDougall, 1989), after which time productivity declines (Groves, 1974; McDougall, 1989). It has no means of extensive vegetative spread. Tussocks are generally ®re-resistant, tillers resprouting after summer ®res from protected basal apices, even when burnt annually (Morgan, in prep). Aerial tillers form when swards remain undisturbed and these are easily damaged by trampling (McDougall, 1989). The ability of tussocks and tillers to recover from ®re after a long period of ®re exclusion is virtually unknown, although in a companion study, Lunt and Morgan (1998) found that post- ®re recovery of Themeda in areas unburnt for 17 yr lagged behind that of a grassland burnt more frequently. Longevity of tussocks is unknown in Victorian grasslands; Morgan (1998b) observed little mortality and turnover of Themeda tussocks over a 3 yr period in a biennially burnt grassland. Seed set occurs primarily in mid-summer (January; McDougall, 1989) but germination does not occur until spring (October) when soil moisture is high and soil temperatures are >20C (Hagon, 1976). A thick litter layer of Themeda inhibits germination; seedlings are generally only observed after ®re when the insulating vegetation cover and litter layer has been removed (Lock and Milburn, 1971; McDougall, 1989), or when grazed.
+# 2.3. Changes in Themeda tussocks with time-since-®re
+A chronosequence study was used to assess changes in T. triandra tussock structure with the time since last
+{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

+®re. Areas of the reserve that originally supported structurally similar species-poor Themeda grassland at the time of reservation in 1985 (Lunt, 1990a), and that subsequently diered in their ®re histories, were chosen for comparative study.

+The design of this study clearly represents a case of pseudoreplication (Hurlbert, 1984); whilst there was replication of plots within each of the ®re history treatments (each >10 ha in size), there was no replication of the treatments (®re histories) themselves. There was no opportunity to achieve a statistically valid design to experimentally test for the eects of time-since-®re on T. triandra but rather, only the chance to study a single grassland that had, by fate of the management over the last decade, diered in ®re history (i.e. the ``unplanned or natural experiment'' of Diamond (1986)). Sharp boundaries between the dierent ®re zones were clearly discernible on the ground and hence, dierences in tussock attributes between treatments were unlikely to be due to soil factors. Such a design places restrictions on the application of inferential statistics, but need not prevent ecological interpretation of the data and their implications for management of the Derrimut Grassland Reserve.

+In areas that had last been burnt 1, 3, 5 yr ago (number of years are expressed as integers) or had remained unburnt (11 yr since exclusion of disturbance), ®ve 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> quadrats were randomly located in visually homogeneous vegetation over an area of ca. 1 ha and the number of live tussocks, live rooted tillers and in¯orescences of T. triandra were counted in December 1996. Basal circumference of tussocks was also measured. Most tussocks usually had an irregular shape that prevented accurate basal diameter estimates.

+Total root biomass was determined in November 1997 in areas burnt 2, 4 and 12 yr ago. At 2 m intervals along a single transect in visually homogeneous vegetation in each ®re zone, and nearest the closest, large (>10 cm diameter) tussock, one soil core (2 cm diameter - 10 cm depth) was taken within 3 cm of the edge of the tussock. A total of 18 cores were collected per ®re zone. The soil samples were then sieved and rinsed under a jet of water before drying the root matter at 80C for 72 h. It was assumed that most of the roots recovered were from T. triandra, an assumption deemed reasonable given that few other species were observed in the areas sampled.

+Changes in vegetation structure in areas last burnt 0.2, 1, 3, >6 and 11 yr ago were documented using point quadrats (Kent and Coker, 1992). A frame consisting of 10 vertically held 4 mm diameter pins, each 10 cm apart, was randomly placed at 12 locations within each ®re zone (n=120 points per ®re zone) and all hits of both live and dead T. triandra, and their height of contact (in 3 cm intervals), were recorded.

+Seasonal changes in above-ground biomass in zones burnt 1, 3 and 11 yr ago were followed for 18 months, from August 1995 to February 1997. At each site, 12 random 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> quadrats were selected at 4±6 week intervals for six months, and then again 12 months later, and all vegetation was cut to ground level, dried at 80C for 48 h and weighed. It was assumed that most (>90%) of the biomass was that of T. triandra, an assumption likely to be valid given that (1) few other species occurred in the areas sampled and (2) the high representation of T. triandra in the biomass samples hand sorted by McDougall (1989) in a similar grassland nearby.

+The comparative ability of Themeda tussocks to recover from ®re was assessed by burning a 1 ha area, unburnt for 12 yr, and an equivalent area most recently burnt 4 yr previously. Both areas were burnt in November 1997. In April 1998, the total number of rooted tillers and tussocks, tussock basal circumference and visual percent cover were recorded in ®ve randomly placed 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> quadrats at each site.
+# 2.4. Statistical analyses

+The number of tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> , number of live tillers, average number of tillers per tussock (square root transformed), number of in¯orescences (square root transformed), average number of in¯orescences per tussock and mean basal circumference were compared between ®re zones that diered in their time-since-®re by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's post-hoc comparisons (Zar, 1984). Homogeneity of variance assumptions were tested using Cochrane's Test (Winer et al., 1991). A mixed-model nested ANOVA was used to test whether basal circumference was aected by site history, with quadrats nested within ®re zones (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981). The Gtest of independence was used to test whether basal circumference, when grouped into size classes, was associated with ®re history (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981). Root biomass dierences with ®re history were compared using a one-way ANOVA on log transformed data with Tukey's post-hoc comparisons.

+Attributes of post-®re recovery of areas previously unburnt for 4 and 12 yr (i.e. number of tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> , number of tillers, average number of tillers per tussock, percent cover) were compared using t-tests (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981). Homogeneity of variance assumptions were checked using the Fmax-test (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981) and satis®ed in all cases. A contingency table was used to test whether basal circumference, when grouped into size classes, was associated with ®re history. Expected values were calculated based on the null hypothesis of independence and tested using the chi-square statistic (Zar, 1984). Standardised residuals were examined to determine the pattern of association between the variables.

+### 3. Results

+All of the above-ground tussock attributes, except basal circumference, signi®cantly declined with increasing time-since-®re (Table 1). There were no signi®cant dierences in tussock attributes between areas burnt 1 and 3 yr previously. Rather, the eects were signi®cant when grasslands had remained unburnt for 55 yr.

+The total number of tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> was lowest in the long unburnt area (11 yr; F=7.10, p=0.003) but did not dier signi®cantly between areas burnt more recently (45 yr). Total number of tillers and mean number of tillers per tussock were highest in 1 and 3 yr unburnt areas, intermediate, but signi®cantly lower, in the 5 yr unburnt area, and least in the 11 yr unburnt area (F=35.32, p < 0.0001 and F=10.54, p< 0.001 respectively). In¯orescence production (total and mean number per tussock) declined with time-since-®re in a similar way (F=47.91, p< 0.0001 and F=16.82, p< 0.001 respectively). Tussock circumference did not dier within (F=0.926, p=0.540) or between (F=1.464, p=0.224) any of the ®re zones, nor was the size class distribution of tussocks signi®cantly associated with time-since-®re (<sup>2</sup> =12.07, n=12, p> 0.05). Thus, all tussock size classes were represented in all ®re zones in similar ratios.

+Mean root biomass (1SE) in the 12 yr unburnt area (0.174 0.019 g/100 cm<sup>3</sup> ; F=26.19, p < 0.001) was less than 45% of that in the areas burnt two (0.432 0.016 g/100 cm<sup>3</sup> ) and four (0.384 0.023 g/100 cm<sup>3</sup> ) years previously, which did not dier from one another (p > 0.05).

+While the total number of contacts with live Themeda did not increase greatly in the years 1 to >6 after burning in the point quadrat study (Fig. 1), the spatial distribution of live leaves in the canopy changed dramatically (Fig. 2). Immediately after ®re, Themeda resprouted rapidly from the base and live leaves were mostly concentrated near the ground level (46 cm) during year 1. In years 2 to >6, the canopy of live leaves elevated higher in each year so that by >6 yr, most of the live canopy was >18 cm above ground level. During the same period, live leaves disappeared completely from tussock bases (<3 cm) and dead vegetation accumulated from the `bottom up' (Fig. 2). At >6 yr after ®re, 73% of all Themeda leaves in the canopy were dead. After 11 yr without disturbance, the grassland appeared to collapse upon itself (Fig. 2). Dead vegetation remained on the soil surface (in a thick layer to 12 cm deep) whilst almost no live vegetation existed at any layer in the canopy.

+Over the 18 months in which above-ground biomass was followed, areas unburnt for 1 and 3 yr at the start of observations increased their total biomass by 167% and 152%, respectively (Fig. 3), within the context of large seasonal variation. During the same time, the total biomass of the area unburnt for 11 yr declined to 58% of its original amount. The decline was most dramatic between February 1997 and February 1998 when biomass fell from 707 g mÿ<sup>2</sup> to 462 g mÿ<sup>2</sup> , despite large increases in biomass at the other two sites. This decline corresponded with the grassland collapse observed in areas which had remained unburnt for >12 yr.

+Time-since-®re aected the subsequent ability of Themeda tussocks to recover from ®re (Table 2). The canopy of the long unburnt area (12 yr since ®re) regrew more slowly (7% versus 35%), had fewer tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> , had fewer tillers and fewer tillers per tussock than the area that had a shorter inter-®re interval (4 yr since ®re; Table 2). +### 4. Discussion

+It has long been recognised that frequent biomass removal by burning is necessary to maintain native plant diversity in ungrazed, species-rich grassland remnants on the western volcanic plains in southern Victoria (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Scarlett and Parsons, 1982; Stuwe, 1986). Where inter-®re intervals exceed 5 yr, even on only rare occasions, competitive exclusion by the dominant tussock grass (T. triandra) has usually been considered to reduce native plant diversity (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Scarlett and Parsons, 1990). This decline may be irreversible given that the soil seed bank type possessed by many native species is a transient one (Lunt, 1995, 1996; Morgan, 1995, 1998a). This study suggests that frequent biomass removal is also necessary to maintain the health and vigour of the dominant grass itself at one of the few reserves dedicated to the conservation of this threatened community (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994).

+The eect of `time-since-®re' on Themeda was the speci®c parameter of interest in this study, but it is confounded with another ®re regime factor, namely, the ®re frequency (Morrison et al., 1995). Some areas experienced no ®res in the 12 yr since reservation, others only one ®re, and yet other areas experienced three ®res in the same period. Although the eects of ®re frequency on Themeda tussocks should not be discounted, given that all ®re zones were generally similar at the time of reservation and that the number of ®res experienced at all sites was low, the parameter of time-since- ®re would appear to be a valid one to compare between ®re zones.

+When time-since-®re exceeded 6 yr, the total number of tillers, number of tillers per tussock and number of in¯orescences per tussock all declined substantially. Whilst the total number of live leaves in the canopy was relatively constant between yr 2 and 6 after ®re, the canopy was raised high above the soil surface with a consequent accumulation of dead leaves around the tussock base. In the prolonged absence of ®re (by 11 yr),

+tussock degeneration becomes substantial; few live tussocks survive in the grassland and the canopy collapses on itself. At 11 yr after ®re, the grassland consists mainly of a dead, slowly decomposing thatch, with little live above-ground material and a markedly declining productivity. The decline was mirrored below-ground where root biomass was also substantially lower than in areas burnt more recently. McDougall (1989) reported the beginnings of tussock decline in a T. triandra grassland reserve nearby after 10 yr of ®re exclusion and we have observed similar processes in other Themeda grasslands in western Victoria, Gippsland and the Australian Capital Territory. Hence, the phenomenon is likely to have some generality in Themeda-dominated grasslands in south-eastern Australia. The rate of tussock decline will undoubtedly vary between sites, and depend chie¯y on site productivity. Interestingly, similar responses to ®re and grazing exclusion have also been reported for T. triandra elsewhere and this suggests that it is a feature of the species itself, rather than a local eect restricted to southern Australia. Mott and Andrew (1985), for instance, found that T. triandra tussocks senesced rapidly after 3 yr without ®re in a tropical savanna in north-west Australia whilst Belsky (1992) has reported that T. triandra can decline in less than 5 yr in the absence of disturbance in a tropical grassland in East Africa.

+The causes of Themeda tussock decline with increasing time-since-®re were not studied here and are poorly understood. It is suspected that shading (i.e. light quantity) at the soil surface, due to the increase in above-ground biomass with time-since-®re, may be a primary cause of tussock decline, as has been reported in other productive grasslands (e.g. Hulbert, 1969; Old, 1969; Knapp and Seastedt, 1986). Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) at the ground surface can be <5% of PAR available above the canopy in Themeda grasslands unburnt for >4 yr (Morgan, 1997), due to the re¯ection and absorption of energy by the standing plant material (Knapp, 1984). Hence, the need to elevate the photosynthetic surface high above the ground increases with time-since-®re as biomass accumulates from the ground up. Some Themeda tillers have the ability to elevate well above the soil surface (described as `aerial tillering' by McDougall (1989)) to reach the light, but many tillers do not successfully compete for light in this way, leading to the loss of live tillers and the resources that are captured by the tussock. A point is reached (by 11 yr after ®re) when aerial tillers can no longer be elevated higher on their weak stems and the canopy collapses. The dead material forms a thick thatch that eectively mulches the soil and prevents seedling regeneration (Lock and Milburn, 1971; McDougall, 1989) and new tiller initiation.

+Other factors that potentially contribute to Themeda tussock decline with increasing time-since-®re also re¯ect the eects that standing dead and litter material have on microclimate at the tussock bases. Two factors appear to warrant further consideration, namely: (i) the eects of red:far red light (i.e. light quality) (Deregibus et al., 1985) and, (ii) below- and above-ground temperatures (Old, 1969; Knapp, 1984). Both factors have been implicated in the abilities of other tussock grasses to initiate new tillers, with modi®cations in light quality by a dense grassland canopy being particularly detrimental to tiller populations of some other C4 grasses (Deregibus et al., 1985).

+After a long ®re-free period (12 yr), a single ®re did not, in the short-term, return the grassland's tussock structure to a state more characteristic of a site with a shorter inter-®re interval (i.e. 4 yr). There were fewer tillers and tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> in the long unburnt site six months after ®re relative to the shorter ®re-interval site and, in general, the tussock structure resembled that in the pre-®re grassland. The rate of Themeda canopy recovery was also slower in the long unburnt area. This has also been observed in a nearby grassland when ®re was reintroduced after 17 yr (Lunt and Morgan, 1998). Slow vegetative recovery probably results because pre- ®re tiller health was poor, with many aerial tillers being killed by ®re, and hence, the subsequent regrowth is from the relatively few, newly initiated tillers found at the soil surface. Regrowth from tillers in the more frequently burnt areas, however, is more likely to be from the recovery of existing tillers, protected by the densely crowded meristems in the basal tuft (Morgan, 1998b). Whether Themeda tussock recovery in the long unburnt area continues in the subsequent post-®re yr, enabling the grassland to more closely resemble the frequently burnt area, is unknown. At the nearby Laverton North Grassland Reserve, however, areas burnt after 17 yr of ®re exclusion appear to retain their dierences (i.e. low tussock density, less canopy cover) at 3 yr after burning compared to adjacent areas burnt more frequently (Morgan, pers. observation).

+grassland structure may aect the habitat suitability of the site for the endangered Delma impar (Striped Legless Lizard), a species largely dependent on the western volcanic plains grassland community. The animal's habitat requirements have not been conclusively determined (e.g. Coulson, 1990; Moro, 1990) but are presumed to revolve around the dense Themeda cover that develops in the yr after ®re. Further research is clearly needed to identify the structural requirements most favoured by D. impar, perhaps using a technique similar to the point quadrat method used here to quantify grassland structure. However, it is apparent from this study that excluding ®re for long periods is likely to cause sward deterioration and hence, potential habitat loss for this species in the long-term.

+Secondly, Themeda sward health may play a role in resisting invasion into the grassland by the aggressive alien perennial grass Nassella neesiana (Lunt and Morgan, submitted). Nassella neesiana is perhaps the most serious environmental weed in remnant native grasslands in southern Victoria (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994; McLaren et al., 1998) and poses a major threat to the conservation of this endangered ecosystem. When Themeda swards are productive and dense (>50% live cover) and tussock densities are high, invasion appears to be inhibited relative to areas where the Themeda sward cover is low and/or unhealthy (Lunt and Morgan, submitted). Leaving grassland areas unburnt for long periods is likely to increase the potential for, and rate of, invasion by N. neesiana because of the decline in vigour and competitive ability of Themeda. Maintenance of a healthy sward of Themeda may prove to be an extremely cost-eective method of slowing (but not preventing) invasion by N. neesiana at Derrimut.

+In summary, the productive, ungrazed grassland at Derrimut requires frequent biomass removal via ®re if the structural dominant (T. triandra) is to remain in a vigourous state. Short inter-®re intervals (i.e. <5 yr intervals) will allow Themeda to maintain its competitiveness and the habitat values it provides for endangered vertebrates in the long-term. Burning will also bene®t an inter-tussock native ¯ora that can be rapidly eliminated from grasslands due to severe competition from Themeda in the absence of disturbance. Frequent ecological burning is therefore likely to be a far more cost-eective conservation management option at Derrimut than the current practice of intermittent, and largely unplanned, burning. When the time between ecological burns exceeds 5±6 yr, however, substantial costs are likely to be incurred to (a) restore degenerate Themeda swards again to a healthy condition and, (b) control aggressive perennial weeds that ¯ourish with long inter-®re intervals. Such activities are non-sustainable in the long-term and importantly, they are almost entirely avoidable in the short-term.

+# **INTRODUCTION**

+The natural fire regimes of the treeless high mountain vegetation of Australia are difficult to quantify, and the role of fire in the dynamics of alpine and subalpine vegetation in Australia is largely unknown. At the landscape scale (that of square kilometres or more), fire appears to be relatively rare in these environments (Kirkpatrick & Dickinson 1984; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Wimbush & Forrester 1988; Williams & Costin 1994). Given that few fires have occurred in alpine and subalpine vegetation, knowledge of post-fire ecology, especially initial impacts and early responses, in alpine and treeless subalpine vegetation is also scant.

+Aboriginal people utilized the high country, but little is known about their use of fire there. Good evidence exists for fire-stick farming in lowlands surrounding high mountains, but there is little evidence for the extensive use of fire, or even the need to use fire extensively, in the treeless vegetation (Flood 1980). Prior to European settlement, landscape-scale fires are likely to have occurred in high mountain treeless vegetation in mainland Australia only once or twice per century (Leigh *et al*. 1987). European settlement in and around the high country commenced in the mid-19th century. +# Early post-fire regeneration in subalpine heathland and grassland in the Victorian Alpine National Park, south-eastern Australia
+C-H. A. WAHREN,1† W. A. PAPST2‡ AND R. J. WILLIAMS<sup>3</sup> \*

+1 *Department of Agricultural Sciences, La Trobe University, Victoria,* <sup>2</sup> *Centre for Land Protection Research, Bendigo, Victoria and* <sup>3</sup> *CSIRO Sustainable Ecosystems, PMB 44, Winnellie Northern Territory 0822, Australia (Email: dick.williams@terc.csiro.au)*

+**Abstract** Landscape fire (at the scale of square kilometres or more) is relatively rare in the alpine and subalpine environments of Australia. In early 1998, a major fire (the 'Caledonia Fire'), burnt approximately 35 000 ha, of which approximately 3000 hectares was subalpine heathland, grassland and wetland within the Victorian Alpine National Park. This fire was one of only three landscape-scale fires that have occurred anywhere in the treeless vegetation of the Victorian Alps in the past 100 years, the others being in 1939 and 1985. Monitoring of regeneration in subalpine vegetation commenced 3 weeks postfire. Sites were established in burnt grassland at Holmes Plain (1400 m a.s.l.) and burnt grassland and heathland at Wellington Plain (1480 m a.s.l.), and in unburnt grassland at both sites. In burnt grassland and heathland, the fire consumed much of the vegetation, leaving extensive areas of bare ground. The cover of dense vegetation declined from > 70% prefire, to approximately 15% immediately postfire. Bare ground at the Holmes and Wellington Plains sites ranged from 70% to 85% immediately postfire. By May 2000, approximately 2.5 years postfire, dense vegetation cover in grassland had increased to approximately 20%, and bare ground had decreased to an average of approximately 30%. In unburnt grassland, dense vegetation cover was generally > 95%, and the amount of bare ground less than 5%. The tussock-forming snow grasses resprouted vigorously following fire, and had flowered prolifically after 1 year. In heathland, most of the shrubs were incinerated, leaving close to 100% bare soil. Since then, a number of grasses and some dominant shrubs have resprouted vigorously, with some seedling regeneration. By May 2000, in heathland, bare soil was still > 50% and dense vegetation < 20%. Such ground cover conditions during this early postfire period were well below prefire levels, and well below the levels necessary to protect alpine soils from erosion. The Caledonia Fire has provided a rare opportunity to study ecological processes associated with postfire regeneration in treeless subalpine landscapes.

+1954; Carr & Turner 1959a; Lawrence 1999). These practices all increased the frequency of fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation (Pryor 1939; Stretton 1946; Raeder-Roitzsch & Phillips 1958; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Banks 1989; Kershaw & Strickland 1989; Lawrence 1999). On mainland Australia, prescribed fire in treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation was banned in the 1940s and 1950s, as its use was linked clearly to land degradation in the high mountain catchments (Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin *et al*. 1959; Williams & Costin 1994).

+In Victoria, there are few detailed data on the occurrence of fires and their effects on alpine and subalpine plant communities. Extensive fires in treeless vegetation are known to have occurred on two occasions in the 20th century. According to Carr & Turner (1959a) '. . . small fires spread onto the high plains from the neighbouring slopes prior to 1939, such as in 1926, but these fires were of minor importance'. In contrast, the State-wide fires of 1939 burnt approximately 80% of the snow gum country on the Bogong High Plains above approximately 1500 m a.s.l. (Carr & Turner 1959a). Although these fires burnt much treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation, that is, heathland, grassland, and wetland (Carr & Turner 1959a), we do not know the precise extent or severity of these fires. In 1985, a fire at Mount Buffalo burnt approximately 11 000 ha of lowland and forested foothill vegetation, and approximately 150 ha of treeless subalpine heathland, grassland and wetland (Wahren *et al*. 1999). The subject of the present paper is an extensive fire that occurred in the south-eastern parts of the Victorian Alpine National Park in January 1998: the 'Caledonia Fire'.

+Subsequent to the last glaciation, Australian alpine environments have evolved in response to relatively small-scale disturbances (1 m<sup>2</sup> –1 ha) such as localized frost heave, wind blasting and insect herbivory. Larger scale disturbances such as fire and extensive grazing by large vertebrate herbivores over square kilometres of country are rare or non-existent (Williams 1990; Williams & Costin 1994). Under such a native regime of small-scale disturbances, Australian alpine environments are characterized by a high cover of vegetation (normally close to 100%) and relatively little exposed bare soil (< 1–2%; Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin 1958; Williams & Costin 1994). The removal of vegetation and litter by fire, and the consequent exposure of bare soil, has major implications in Australian alpine landscapes, because exposure of alpine soils is undesirable for soil conservation purposes, and subsequent regeneration to adequate soil cover is slow (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).

+In the present paper, we summarize the early postfire changes in vegetation and ground cover conditions that have occurred in grassland and heathland on Holmes and Wellington Plains, two of the larger high plains burnt in the Caledonia Fire (Fig. 1). We focus on the first 2 years post-fire because there have been no detailed, quantitative studies of early post-fire responses in Australian alpine landscapes following fires of such magnitude. The specific aim is to document the changes in vegetation cover, the amount of bare ground, and changes to gaps that have occurred in grassland and heathland over the first 2 years post-fire. Both communities are extensive in treeless high mountain environments in Australia. Within each, the amount of bare ground and both the quality and quantity of vegetation cover, and the nature of gaps created by the death of grass tussocks or shrubs, are critical determinants of both vegetation change and landscape condition in Australian high mountain landscapes (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).
+#### **Fire and study sites**

+The Caledonia Fire started on 31 December 1997, from an abandoned campfire on the Caledonia River, in mixed lowland eucalypt forest. 1 January 1998 was a day of extreme fire weather: the predicted forest fire danger index (Luke & McArthur 1978) for the nearby town of Heyfield was 50 (Tolhurst 1998). Fire weather and drought conditions at this time were broadly similar to those of other years in the past century when widespread fires occurred in Victoria: 1983, 1967, 1964, 1939 and 1926 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000). The fire burnt approximately 35 000 ha of the Carey Forest, of which approximately 22 000 ha was within the Alpine National Park, and approximately 3000 ha was treeless subalpine vegetation.

+The landscape above approximately 1400 m is a mosaic of high ridges, wooded slopes, rolling grassy plains and wetlands. The treeless plains and surrounding snow gum (*Eucalyptus pauciflora*) woodlands have been grazed during summer and autumn by free ranging cattle since the late 19th century and cattle were present at the time of the fire. Sporadic grazing continued for 3 months post-fire, but grazing was excluded from the fire-affected area for the 1998–1999 and 1999–2000 seasons.

+The fires were intense crown fires in both the eucalypt forests of the foothills and the subalpine snow gum woodlands. In the treeless vegetation, fire intensity was unknown, but field observations indicated that the fire at Wellington Plain was more intense and burnt more of the vegetation than at Holmes Plain. At Holmes and Wellington Plains, > 90% of the grassland, heathland and snow gum woodlands were burnt, and the subalpine bogs were also extensively burnt. This represents the most extensive fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation since 1939 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000).

+# **METHODS**
+#### **Monitoring sites**

+At the end of January 1998, 3 weeks after the fire, monitoring sites were established at Holmes Plain (146°45-14--E, 37°24-32--S; 1400 m a.s.l.) and Wellington Plain (146°49-54--E, 37°29-46--S; 1480 m a.s.l.). These plains were selected because they were representative of the extensive subalpine high plains in this region of the Victorian Alps (Walsh *et al*. 1984, 1986) and, in the case of Holmes Plain, because two sites had been established in grassland in 1991 as part of a general monitoring program in the high country. At both sites, the soil was alpine humus soil, a wellstructured organic loam that is acid, nutrient poor, and is typical of most alpine and subalpine grasslands and heathlands in mainland Australia (Williams & Costin 1994). One of these sites was burnt, the other was outside the fire perimeter; both sites were used for the present study. Extra sites were established in burnt heathland and grassland at both Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in an unburnt area of grassland at Wellington Plain, close to the burnt grassland. This unburnt grassland was within the fire perimeter. Using this network of sites, the changes in the burnt grassland over time could be compared with those in longunburnt grassland. Unfortunately, there were no suitable unburnt heathland sites.
+# **Estimation of ground cover and biomass**

+Point quadrats, sampled along permanent transects (Kent & Coker 1992), were used to record species composition and ground cover conditions. Transects were 10 m long with points 4 mm in diameter, and 20 cm apart (50 points per transect). This method has been widely used for many decades to estimate the cover of individual species and life forms (grasses, forbs and shrubs) in treeless vegetation in Australia (Carr & Turner 1959b; Wimbush & Costin 1979a,b,c; Wahren *et al*. 1994). Ground cover at each point was rated in terms of three cover classes (Wahren *et al*. 1994). Cover class 1 (CC1) is fixed litter or dense live vegetation, cover class (CC2) provides intermediate vegetation cover but the litter is loose, and cover class (CC3) consists of bare ground or sparse vegetation and/or thin (< 5 mm thick) loose litter. Live vegetation and litter were measured together in all cover classes, as both are important for soil protection in Australian alpine environments (Wahren *et al*. 1994).

+In the Holmes Plain grassland, there were 40 transects (including 13 from 1991) distributed over an area of approximately 40 ha of burnt grassland. There were an additional 10 transects (six from 1991) in the unburnt grassland, over an area of approximately 2 ha; burnt and unburnt grassland sites were approximately 1 km apart. At Wellington Plain, there were 40 transects established in burnt heathland over an area of approximately 40 ha, and 10 transects in burnt grassland over an area of 2 ha. Subsequent to January 1998, the vegetation was remeasured along the transects in May 1998, January, May and December 1999, and late April/early May 2000. In December 1999, four transects were set up in a patch of unburnt grassland at Wellington Plain, 200 m from the burnt grassland; these were remeasured in May 2000.

+Above-ground biomass was sampled in March–May 2000, using direct harvest from 10 0.25-m<sup>2</sup> quadrats distributed at random in both burnt and unburnt grassland of Holmes and Wellington Plains. Samples were separated in the field into standing vegetation and litter components. Biomass samples were not collected from heathland because of the likely damage to regenerating areas where there was at least 50% bare ground and small shrub seedlings.
+#### **Assessment of grass tussock basal area, intertussock gaps and prefire shrub cover**

+In addition to changes in bare ground and vegetation cover, we documented changes in the size and type of gap, both interdominant and within-canopy, in grassland and heathland. Such gaps are important determinants of ecological processes in these communities (Williams & Ashton 1988; Williams 1992). The area occupied by intertussock gaps and *Poa* tussock bases was estimated by line intercepts (Bonham 1989). Intercepted basal tussock length was measured by using a metal pin, 4 mm in diameter, placed vertically against the edge of the tussock. Ten randomly distributed 10-m long transects were sampled in both burnt and unburnt grassland at Holmes Plain, and in burnt grassland at Wellington Plain. As there were no prefire data of shrub cover in open heathland, this was estimated at Holmes Plain by using line intercepts to determine the diameter of burnt shrubs, based on the extent of burnt branches. This method could not be applied at Wellington Plain because the fire had incinerated most shrubs, leaving few or no stems.
+# **Data analysis**

+Point quadrat data were explored using box and normal probability plots (Sokal & Rohlf 1995), which showed that all data met the assumptions for ANOVA. As the vegetation was sampled at the same sets of transects over time, we used repeated measures ANOVA (von Ende 1993). Mean intertussock gap size and mean tussock basal size, in burnt and unburnt grassland, were
+{3}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
+analysed by one-way ANOVA, whereas the biomass data were analysed by two-way (site fire) ANOVA. All analyses were undertaken using SYSTAT 8.0 (SPSS, Chicago).
+#### **RESULTS**
+## **Immediate fire impact**

+The Caledonia Fire affected most vegetation and all plant communities of both Holmes and Wellington Plains. The main impact was removal of vegetative cover and litter, resulting in high levels of bare ground and little vegetation cover. In burnt grassland at Holmes Plain, the average amount of CC1 was 17%, and the average amount of CC3 was 76%. This was a substantial decrease in the quality of cover at Holmes Plain compared with the prefire state (Fig. 2a). In burnt grassland at Wellington Plain, the respective figures were 11 and 85% (Fig. 2b). In burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, all shrubs were incinerated, resulting in virtually no vegetation (CC1 = 3%) and an almost complete cover of bare ground (CC3 = 96%; Fig. 2b).
+# **Post-fire regeneration**
+#### *Changes in vegetation cover and biomass*

+In burnt grassland, both at Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, CC1 increased significantly, and CC3 decreased significantly over the 2.5-year study period, with most of the changes occurring in the first 18 months post-fire. There was a significant change in both CC1 and CC3 between February 1998 and May 1999, but between May 1999 and May 2000, there was little or no significant change in the average value of either cover class across sites (Fig. 2a). Similarly, there were significant changes in the cover classes in both grassland and heathland at Wellington Plain between January 1998 and May 1999, but relatively little change between May 1999 and May 2000 (Fig. 2b). By May 2000, the average CC3 in burnt grassland was 35% at Holmes Plain (Fig. 2a) and 25% at Wellington Plain (Fig. 2b). The respective figures for CC1 were 23 and 36%. In burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, average CC3 in May 2000 was 53%, and average CC1 was 16% (Fig. 2b).

+The post-fire increase in vegetation cover at both Holmes and Wellington Plains was primarily due to the rapid resprouting of snow grass tussocks and forbs (Figs 3a,4). The cover of *Poa* increased rapidly postfire in both grassland and heathland. At Holmes Plain it was 84% by January 1999 (Fig. 3a); at Wellington

+Plain it was approximately 65% in grassland by May 1999, and 55% in heathland (Fig. 4a,b). *Poa* cover remained at or near these levels at both sites until May 2000. This cover was almost completely due to surviving tussocks resprouting post-fire, rather than seedling establishment and growth. The rapid resprouting of the snow grasses was accompanied by pyrogenic flowering, which commenced in the year following the fire and occurred in virtually all tussocks. Forbs also re-established rapidly from perennating subterranean organs or seedlings. Forb cover was approximately 40% by January 1999 at both grassland sites, and by December 1999 at the heathland site (Figs 3a,4). Most forb cover was provided by *Asperula gunnii, Craspedia* spp. and *Leptorhynchos squamatus*. Some, such as *Bracteantha subundulata* and *Podolepis robusta*, occurred in distinct patches of 0.5–3 m<sup>2</sup> .

+In contrast to the rapid regeneration of snow grasses and forbs, shrubs in the heathland of Wellington Plain were slow to regenerate (Fig. 4b). Shrub cover increased at approximately 7% per annum, such that by May 2000, shrub cover was 17%. Although the prefire shrub cover at this site is unknown, it is likely to have been at least 50%, as the area had been mapped as closed heathland by Walsh *et al*. (1984). Shrubs, including the dominants, whether seedlings or resprouts, had not flowered after 2.5 years.

+The cover classes at the various prefire or unburnt grassland sites showed some intersite variation across the landscape and over time. In 1991 at Holmes Plain, at one site that was subsequently burnt in 1998, CC1 was 49% and CC3 was 21% (Fig. 2a). At the first site, total live vegetation cover was 80%, of which *Poa* provided three-quarters of the cover and forbs approximately one-quarter. The intertussock gaps at this site were generally occupied by forbs only, with little or no live grass foliage overlapping the gap, and only sparse litter within the gap. At the second site, unburnt by the Caledonia Fire, the respective CC1 and CC3 values in 1991 were 69 and 3%, and 73 and 5% in February

+In open heathland at Holmes Plain, the estimated prefire cover of *Grevillea australis* was approximately 20%. These *Grevillea* shrubs were killed and the litter beneath their canopies, which is normally thick (up to 5 cm) and loose, was completely burnt. +# **DISCUSSION**
+#### **Fire regimes in alpine and subalpine environments in Australia**

+The available historical, meteorological and biological evidence points strongly to landscape-scale fire being a relatively rare event in Australian alpine and subalpine vegetation. McCarthy and Tolhurst (2000) estimated that the fire-weather conditions associated with the Caledonia Fire have occurred five times in the past century. Assuming a relative lack of ignition sources in treeless high mountain vegetation compared with

+forest vegetation, they concluded that a fire frequency of once or twice per century was 'a reasonable prediction'. In subalpine areas in the ACT and NSW, the data of Pryor (1939) and Raeder-Roitzsch and Phillips (1958) are consistent with this conclusion.

+This relatively low frequency of fire in Australian alpine landscapes is a function of the generally low to moderate fire weather conditions that occur at high altitude compared with landscapes at lower altitudes (Gill & Moore 1990). Fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation occurs only in exceptional circumstances, such as when drought is coupled with extreme fire-weather conditions. The fire discussed here has therefore provided a rare opportunity for detailed monitoring, in both the immediate post-fire period and the longer term, of the ecological processes governing post-fire vegetation change in high mountain treeless vegetation.
+# **Post-fire patterns of regeneration**

+The most conspicuous response to fire was the rapid resprouting of most species. The vast majority of the alpine vascular flora has the capacity to resprout, from rhizomes or rootstock, and other perennating buds are generally protected by foliage and occur close to the ground (Williams & Costin 1994). This early onset of regeneration following fire is common in many ecosystems, and is often a function of increased soil nutrients in combination with a more open habitat and reduced competition (Gill 1981; Clarkson 1997; DeBano *et al*. 1998). In the Alps, such strong vegetative regeneration post-fire, however, is most likely an adaptation to the exigencies of the alpine climate rather than an adaptation to fire per se.

+In the grasslands and heathlands, there was massed pyrogenic flowering of snow grasses, a phenomenon that is relatively common in the first year or two postfire in alpine and subalpine grasses (Leigh *et al*. 1987; Yeates & Lee 1997). In the burnt grasslands and heathlands, such flowering will naturally provide a significant input to the soil seed-bank.

+Based on 1991 figures, the cover of snow grasses and forbs had returned to approximately prefire levels by May 1999 (17 months post-fire). These responses occurred on both Holmes and Wellington Plain. This initial burst of regeneration was accompanied by a relatively rapid initial decline in the amount bare ground and/or thin loose litter with little vegetation cover (CC3) compared with the high values immediately post-fire.

+Despite this rapid resprouting, and the return of total grass and forb cover to prefire levels within 2.5 years, the amount of CC3 (25–53%) was well above, whereas the amount of dense vegetation cover (CC1, 16–36%) was well below, levels typical for grassland and heathland in an unburnt state. At the majority of unburnt sites currently being monitored in the study area, the Holmes and Wellington Plains sites, and at independent sites at Wellington Plain and Mount Reynard (A. Tolsma, University of Melbourne School of Forestry, unpubl. data), vegetation cover was in excess of 95%, and bare ground was < 3%. Such values are typical of long unburnt, ungrazed alpine and subalpine vegetation elsewhere in Australia, where bare ground is generally less than 1–2%, and vegetation cover is almost complete (Costin *et al*. 1960; Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994; Williams *et al*. 1997; Wahren & Papst 2000).

+While tussocks and shrubs establish and mature, the burnt grasslands and heathlands of these subalpine plains will remain vulnerable and sensitive to physical disturbances, such as frost heave, and any trampling by livestock. Post-fire regeneration studies from numerous alpine, subalpine or tundra sites around the world (Wimbush & Costin 1979a,b,c; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Racine *et al*. 1987; Gitay *et al*. 1992; Landhausser & Wein 1993; Wahren *et al*. 1994; Maumary *et al*. 1995; Williams *et al*. 1997; Yeates & Lee 1997; Vavrek *et al*. 1999) indicate that recovery to adequate levels of vegetation to protect the soil from subsequent disturbances is likely to take a decade or more. Given such high levels of bare or sparsely covered ground and low levels of vegetation cover in burnt sites, and the general slowness of vegetation regeneration following largescale disturbances in Australian alpine environments, we conclude that the vegetation at Holmes and Wellington Plains has not recovered to prefire levels. Thus, there has been only limited post-fire regeneration, and, 2.5 years after the Caledonia Fire, the potential for soil erosion still exists in the burnt, treeless vegetation.
+# *Patterns in grasslands*

+The biomass (including litter) of burnt grassland 2.5 years post-fire was significantly less than that of unburnt grassland, and less than that considered necessary for adequate protection of alpine soils (10 t ha–1; Costin *et al*. 1960). The litter component of biomass in burnt areas was negligible, whereas in the unburnt grassland, litter constituted almost half the biomass. Litter performs a crucial role in alpine environments, because it blankets the soils against extremes of temperature, and is a major source of organic matter that is an important determinant of soil chemical and physical health (Baldock & Nelson 2000). Such litter, much of which occurs in intertussock gaps, was totally consumed by the fire.

+In grasslands, fire not only consumed litter, but resulted in a significant decline in the basal cover of snow grass tussocks and an increase in the size of intertussock gaps. By May 2000, the vegetation of these gaps was relatively sparse, with little dense cover. Thus, by
+{8}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

+increasing the size of the gaps, and consuming the litter within the gaps, fire has increased the potential area of sparse ground cover and therefore the potential for soil erosion. As regeneration in alpine communities is generally slow, the return of the litter component and the centripetal in-filling of gaps in the grasslands will take several more years.
+# *Patterns in heathlands*

+Most shrubs were incinerated, as was the thick litter beneath the shrub canopy, causing almost 100% bare ground. Resprouting in the shrubs was slower than that of the herbaceous species. *Grevillea australis*, a shrub that is a known obligate seeder (Williams & Ashton 1988), was killed by 100% leaf scorch. Despite the decrease in the amount of bare ground in heathland post-fire, by May 2000 it was still high (mean 53%, pooling sites).

+Whether or not a return to prefire state occurs will depend mainly on species, mode of regeneration and subsequent disturbance regime (e.g. Gill 1981; DeBano *et al*. 1998). Where *Grevillea* seedlings established, they were still < 10 cm tall 2.5 years post-fire, and development to mature shrubs will take a decade or more (Williams & Ashton 1987, 1988). Other postfire regeneration studies in heathland elsewhere in the Victorian Alps, such as at Mount Fainter and Mount Buffalo (Wahren *et al*. 1999), have shown that recovery of heathland to prefire levels of vegetation cover (including litter) and bare ground is likely to take 10–15 years. As for the grasslands, then, the heathlands will therefore remain sensitive to physical disturbance while plants re-establish and mature.
+# **Conclusion**

+The primary impact of fire in the subalpine landscapes on Holmes and Wellington Plain was, like any fire, the almost total removal of vegetation cover and litter and extensive exposure of bare ground. Such low levels of vegetation cover are highly unusual in virtually all unburnt Australian alpine and subalpine grassland and heathland communities. Although resprouting of herbaceous species following the fire was initially rapid in both grassland and heathland, the amount of vegetation cover in both communities 2.5 years post-fire was still insufficient to protect the soils. Soil and catchment protection is a major land use in the Australian Alps. As has been documented for other subalpine and alpine heathlands and grasslands subject to fire, the development of levels of vegetation and litter that will adequately protect the soil, and hence the catchments, will take a decade or more. The rarity of landscape-scale fire, and the slowness of regeneration post-fire, in treeless vegetation of the Australian Alps is such that the

+lands affected by the Caledonia Fire warrant intensive long-term studies. Such studies are the principal means of gaining an understanding of both species and plant community responses following major but rare disturbances such as a landscape-scale fire.

-# **Conservation of Endangered Plants in Urban Fire-Prone Habitats**
-**Tony D. Auld and Judith Scott**
-*New South Wales National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Nurstville N.S.W. 2220, Australia Tel. +6102 958.5 6497; Fax* **+61** 02 **9585 6495;** *E-mail* **tauld@pws.nsw.gov.au**

-**Abstract.** A number of endangered plant species occur in NationflParks and associated bushland that are adjacent to urban areas in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia. Within these areas fire is a repeated and frequent disturbance event that potentially threatens not only the endangered flora but life and property as well. These threats were well illustrated by the impact of the fires that occurred in January 1994 in Sydney.

-For the management of such fire-prone areas there is a need to identify those fire regimes likely to drive the endangered flora to extinction. Management of fire-sensitive, threatened *Danvinia* (Myrtaceae) and *Grevillea* (Proteaceae) species illustrates how conservation goals can be applied along with protection of life and property. A regime of frequent fue will lead to local population declines and extinction in both *Danvinia* and *Grevillea* species. Consequently, frequent buming on a regular basis for hazard reduction to protect property assets is inappropriate for the conservation of these species. *Danvinia* species also require fires that cause significant soil heating (high consumption of fine fuel) to break seed dormancy in soil stored seed, while *Grevillea* species require fires of a large spatial extent to minimise the impact of mammalian seed predators on seed outputs from the first few seed-crops produced by plants after a fire.
-**Keywords: Fireregime; 'I2xeatenedspecies;Danuinia; Grevillea**
-tect life and property from the dangers posed by fire in urban bushland as well as conserving this biodiversity.

-Given the high potential for extreme fire events, where effective control of wildfire is not always possible (as happened in January 1994), there is increasing pressure for widespread fuel reduction burning in urban bushland adjacent to human assets such as houses. Such areas contain a number of endangered, vulnerable or rare plant species that are of high conservation significance, as well as more common species, all of which will have particular fire requirements which may or may not be compatible with burning for fuel reduction purposes. Hence, there is a potential for a conflict over protection versus conservation priorities (Bradstock, Keith & Auld 1995, Bradstock & Scott 1995). To attempt to resolve such conflicts we must have a sound knowledge of the effects of different fire regimes on plant and animal species and as land managers apply an informed choice of appropriate fire regimes to ensure the maintenance of populations of plants and animals.

-This paper presents data on the effect of different components of the fire regime on several threatened plant species in order to provide land managers with potential conservation prescriptions for threatened plant species. In particular, we identify those fire regimes that may cause populations to decline. Such prescriptions can then be incorporated into planning and the implementation of a fuel reduction program, so that conservation issues are not ignored and fire regimes which threaten plane conservation are avoided.
-#### **Introduction**
-#### **Study Area**

-In the Sydney Region of southeastern Australia, much of the vegetation is highly flammable and fires are a common and frequent event. For example, d-wing January of 1994, some 90% and 65% respectively of the two major, large urban reserves (Royal and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Parks) were burnt. In this rich and diverse floristic area, around 2000 plant species regularly experience fire. As a consequence, the management of fire is one of the principal challenges facing managers of natural ecosystems in the Sydney Region. Managers must attempt to pro-

-The Sydney area in south-eastem Australia is a large urban area fringed with large bushland reserves and containing many smaller reserves (Figure 1). Within this area, the vegetation is dominated by sclerophyll heathlands, woodlands and forests, situated on infertile sandy soils derived from Hawkesbury sandstone (Beadle 1981), in a landscape of dissected sandstone plateaux. Rainfall is mund 1200mm per annum with a peak in late summer. Average monthly maximum/minimum temperatures for
-{1}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
-**Figure 1.** The Sydney urban area and adjacent bushland reserves showing the distribution of *Danvinia* and *GreviIlea* study species.

-Sydney are 26118OC in summer and 16/8"C in winter. **A**  broad range of fire regimes are possible in the Sydney Region. High intensity wildfires occur in the order of once every 5-10 years, while deliberate prescriptions of low intensity fires are commonly used for fuel reduction. Arson is a major source of wildfire ignitions.
-#### **The Fire Regime**

-For the long term survival of plants and animals we need to know how they are affected by the fire regime, ie. (frequency, intensity, season, spatial extent). Here we concentrate on fire-sensitive plants.
-#### *Fire frequency*

-All fires burn areas of vegetation that have been burnt some time before. Consequently, the vegetation is really a mosaic of fire histories, with some parts having had more fires than others over a given time period. We need to try and understand how important this unequal patchiness of fires through time is for the survival of plants.

-Plants that are killed by fire rely on seed germination after fires to survive at a particular location. For these fire-sensitive plants, there must be sufficient time between successive fires for seedlings *to* mature and produce more seeds and hence, add seeds to the seedbank. In the Sydney area, this time will vary between species and loca
-{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

-tions (Benson 1985), from species that flower within 1-2 years after fire (Actinotus helianthi, Acacia suaveolens) to those that may take 4-8 years to reach maturity (Banksia ericifolia). If another fire should occur before these plants have matured, dramatic changes in the vegetation may occur. Fire-sensitive plants with seed stored in woody capsules usually release dl their seeds after a fire and no residual seeds remain in cones. These plants are the group of species most susceptible to two fires in short succession. Plants that have seeds stored in the soil usually have some residual seedbank remaining in the soil following post-fire germination. For these species, a second fire before seedlings mature may severely reduce population numbers but it may not eliminate species locally. However, in some places, after some fires, the entire soil seedbank may be exhausted, eg. Restionaceae and Epacridaceae (Meney et al. 1994), Grevillea (Auld unpubl.) and local extinction will occur if two fires occur close enough together to kill seedlings from the first fire before they are mature. Ideally, as land managers with concerns for the conservation of biodiversity, we should allow the interval between fires to be long enough not only simply for plant species to mature, but at a minimum, several fruiting seasons beyond this so that a sufficiently large seedbank can be established before the next fire occurs.
-# Fire Intensity

-How hot a fire is will depend on how much combustible fuel is available, how dry this fuel is, the topography of the area and the weather conditions, such as humidity and windspeed. When an area is burnt, the important thing for plants and animals is how much heat is produced, and in many areas around Sydney, this usually varies markedly even on a very small scale (i.e., over tens of meters). How much heat a fire produces can affect the survival of plants. In intense fires there is likely to be higher levels of resprouting plants killed, and longer periods needed before the next fire for recovery, than in mild fires. For plants, the more heat produced by a fire, the greater are the opportunities for seedling recruitment and the greater the magnitude of seedlings that are recruited (Auld & 01Connel11991). Many plant species have seeds which lie dormant in the soil and for a number of these the amount of soil heating that occurs during the passage of a fire will govern the degree of germination after the fire. This heat response is widespread in many plant families, particularly legumes, in fire-prone communities throughout the world (Martin et al. 1975, Jeffery et al. 1988, Auld & O'Connell 1991, Keeley 1991). Bradstock and Auld (1995) have shown that in Hawkesbury sandstone soil around Sydney, it is the amount of fine fuel that is consumed during a fire that governs the degree of soil heating.
-# Fire season

-Given the prevalence of arson and widespread hazard reduction burning for the protection of life and property, fires can now be expected to occur at just about any time of the year in the Sydney Region. The question is, for the long-term survival of plants does it matter when the vegetation is burnt? In Sydney, Bradstock and Bedward (1992) have suggested that seedling survival after fire is largely independent of season of burn because rainfall is very variable. Although there is a trend for wetter periods in late summer/autumn and drier periods in spring this pattern is not strong enough to allow accurate predictions about the impact of season of bum on seedling survival post-fire. Perhaps the most critical role season of burning may play is in influencing fire intensity. Fires in the hot dry summer months when fuel moisture is low will generally be of higher intensities than burns in winter when the vegetation is moister, an ambient temperatures are lower.
-# Fire Spatial Extent

-What is the impact of the spatial extent of fires on plants? In Sydney, fires come in all shapes and sizes. Some burn very extensive areas, while others may only burn a hectare or so. Within the boundaries of a burnt area, fires may be widespread and burn most of the vegetation or leave large parts of the vegetation unbumt or simply lightly scorched. All fires will be different, depending on the terrain, rate of fire spread, amount of fuel available and its moisture content and weather conditions and natural or man-made fire breaks. This results in a patchiness of fires in area and intensity.

-For plants, the spatial extent of fires may be important where burns occur on a very small scale (a few hectares). In such cases, native animals from surrounding unburnt vegetation may graze heavily on the new green shoots that appear after fire and hence, cause a decline in some plant species. These native animals may also consume many of the seeds that are produced in the first few years after fire for those fire-sensitive plants that are trying to replenish their soil seedbanks. This will slow the rate of recovery of such plants.
-# **Study Species**

-The threatened species examined, Darwinia spp. (Myrtaceae) and Grevillea spp. (Proteaceae), are all killed by fire (fire-sensitive, see Gill 1981) and rely on germination from a soil seedbank for persistence at a site after a fire. They are all restricted to the vicinity of Sydney (Figure 1). Threat codes are from Briggs and Leigh (1996).
-{3}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

-*Danvinia biflora* (Cheel) B.Briggs. Vulnerable. A small shrub to 1 m in height in woodland communities mainly in the Hornsby Plateau area in the northern suburbs of Sydney and associated with the Hammondville soil group (Burkitt, Wilson & Benson 1984). The largest populations occur in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, with small outliers in Lane Cove National Park, Marramarra National Park and Pennant Hills Park. This species is threatened by habitat loss, disturbance leading to weed invasion and an inappropriate fire regime.

-*Darwinia diminuta* B Briggs. Rare. A small shrub to 60 cm in height in woodland and heath communities. Found on sandstone in a few localities in Royal National Park, Heathcote National Park, Garawarra State Recreation Area and Kelly's Falls to the south of Sydney and Garigal National Park in the northern Sydney suburbs. D. *diminuta* is threatened by habitat loss, site disturbance and an inappropriate fire regime.

-*Darwinia glaucophylla* B. Briggs. Rare. A spreading prostrate shrub in heath. Confined to a few localities on sandstone in the Gosford area north of Sydney. *D. glaucophylla* is threatened by urban development and an inappropriate fire regime.

-*Darwinia procera* B. Briggs. Rare. **An** erect shrub to 2 m in height in heath to open forest communities. Mostly confined to sheltered gullies and creek banks on sandstone. Restricted to a few localities between Garigal NP and Brisbane Water NP, in the northern suburbs of Sydney. *D. procera* is threatened by habitat loss, urban runoff and an inappropriate fire regime.

-*Grevillea caleyi* R.Br. Endangered. A shrub to 4m by 4m occurring on laterite soils in open forests or low open forests and restricted to roughly a *6* **X** *6* km area centred on the northern Sydney suburb of Terrey Hills. Habitat destruction has divided the original distribution of the species into a series of discrete population fragments (Scott et al. 1995) separated by urban development (houses, roads, business parks etc). Some 85% of the former habitat of G. *caleyi* has been lost to urban development. Only two of the remaining sites are relatively undisturbed and only one of these two has any long-term protection as it occurs in Mu-ring-gai Chase National Park. The remaining large patches are highly distwkd. The major threats to the survival of *G. caleyi* arise from human interference in the environment. These threats range from loss of habitat through clearing, urbanisation and associated infrastructure, changes in landuse and an inappropriate fire regime, to localised disturbance at sites including invasion of weed species and the dumping of rubbish (Scott et al. 1995).

-*Grevillea longifolia* R.Br. Rare. *A* bushy shrub 2-4 m in height by the same wide. It is found in the southern half of the Sydney Region and Woronora plateau and the Jamieson Valley of the Blue Mountains. Usually found in moist areas adjacent to creeks in open forest, but wcasionally on escarpments and ridgetops in woodlands on Hawkesbury sandstone. *G. longifolia* is threatened by urban development, runoff, weed encroachment and an inappropriate fire regime.

-*Grevillea shiressii* Blakley. Vulnerable. A bushy shrub 2-5 m in height. Found only on the banks of two creeks in closed forest in Brisbane Water National Park in the north of Sydney on soils derived from Narrabeen group geology. G. *shiressii* is threatened by disturbance (a fire trail passes through one population) and an inappropriate fire regime.
-#### The Effects **of** the Fire Regime on Threatened **Plant** Species

-For all study species, demographic data were collated on IhreatenedDarwiraia and *Grevillea* species (Scott 1986, Auld et al. 1991, Auld et al. 1993, Auld and Tozer 1995, Scott et al. 1995) and the impacts of components of the fire regime were assessed. A summary of the significant demographic characteristics of our threatened study species is presented in Table 1.
-# *Darwinia* spp. (Myrtaceae)

-As the *Darwinia* spp. studied are all killed by fire, a fire-free period is needed after any one fire to allow seedlings to mature and replenish the soil seedbank. Wants can produce a few fruits two years after fire. As plants grow, fecundity increases and for **all** *Darwinia* species, soil seedbanks should increase rapidly 5-1 0 years after a fire. Most of the annually produced seed-crop is released in a viable, dormant state and would be incorporated into this seedbank, although there is some yearly variation in the proportion of non dormant seeds produced (eg. D. *glaucophylla,* Table *1).*

-For *D. hiflora,* some 75% of the dormant seed released in any one annual seed-crop becomes non dormant and has germinated by 24 months after release, i.e., most seeds from any one seed-crop are short-lived in the soil. The seedbank should buildup in the soil rapidly after a site is burnt, but the seedbank will also decline rapidly should adult plants senesce. The low level of seed longevity in the soil in *D. biflora* (Table 1) suggests that both adult survival and the level of adult fecundity are the critical factors that govern persistence of the soil seedbank. As seeds decay rapidly in the soil, adult plants must regularly produce seeds to maintain a soil seedbank. The longevity of annual seed inputs to the soil seedbank is currently unknown for the other *Darwinia* spp. However, for *D. diminuta, D. glaucophylla* and *D. procera* the seedbank size is likely to be much larger than in *D. biflora,*  given the higher fecundity levels in these species (Figure *2).*
-The fate of those seeds in the soil which lose their dormancy and germinate is unknown. It seems likely that

-seedlings which emerge during the inter-fire period do not establish because of competitive pressure from an established cover of shrubs, herbs and grasses (c.f. *Acacia*  spp. Weiss 1984, Auld 1986). Alternatively, some limited on-going establishment could be possible if seedlings were able to tolerate the existing cover of shrubs, herbs and grasses.

-All *Darwinia* spp. showed some breaking of seed dormancy in response to heating. This suggests that the degree of soil heating during the passage of a fire, itself controlled by available fuel loads (Bradstock & Auld 1995), will influence the number of seeds within the seedbank that germinate after a fire. Near the soil surface lethal soil temperatures (>120°C) are likely to cause some seed death. The seedbank of these *Darwinia* spp. will be unaffected in a fire where soil heating is below the critical level needed to break seed dormancy, i.e., fires consuming small quantities of fuel.

-In G. *caleyi* and *G. longijolia,* seedlings do not flower and produce seeds before 2.5-5 years of age. Fecundity is low in G. *caleyi* with only about 3% of flowers resulting in mature seed (Scott 1986). The level of fecundity in both G. *caleyi* and *G. longifolia* increases until around 10 years of age in response to plant growth (Figure 3). No fecundity estimates have been made for G. *shiressii.* Seeds had a high level of viability and were largely released in a dormant .state in *G. caleyi* and *G. shiressii.* In *G. longifolia,* a large fraction of seeds were released in a non dormant state (Table l), although this is variable across populations and years. Predispersal seed predation is known to be high in G. *caleyi* and *G. shiressii* with significant losses to the weevil *Cydmaea dorsalis* Lea (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) in G. *caleyi* and to the wasp *Eurytoma* sp. (Hymenoptera: Eurytomidae) in G. *shiressii.*  In *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia,* seed dispersal is minimal. **At** maturity the fruits dehisce, dropping the seed to the ground beneath the parent plant. The seeds lack any lipid body attachment that would make them attractive to ants (Auld 1995). In contrast, G. *shiressii* seeds have a lipid body attachment and some 28% of seed are dispersed by ants. In all three threatened *Grevillea* spp. and other more common *Grevillea* spp., post-dispersal seed predation is very high (Auld 1995, Auld & Denham in prep.). Most of the seeds lying on the soil surface are consumed by
-# *Grevillea* spp. (Proteaceae)

-All *Grevillea* species studied were killed by fire and relied on seed germination after a fire to maintain population~. For all species, the magnitude of the soil seedbank will be largely controlled by the levels of adult fecundity, mammal seed predation and adult mortality.
-{5}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
-**Figure 2. Fecundity after fire in** *Dawinia.* **a)** *D. biflora;* **b)** *D. diminuta; c) D. glaucophylla;* **and** *d) D. procera.*

-two native mammals, swamp wallabies (Wallabia bicolor) and bush rats (Rattus fuscipes and possibly other Rattus species). As a result, very few of the developing fruits from any one season contribute seeds to the seedbank. The relationship between mammal densities and the size of area burnt needs to be examined. In the past, some G. caleyi sites have been subjected to small patch burns. In these burnt areas, the level of seed losses to mammals was similar to adjacent unburnt areas and the establishment of a soil seedbank was expected to be retarded.

-The major difference between G. caleyi and G. longifolia was the level of adult mortality within a population. Adult mortality was high in G. caleyi, while there was little adult mortality in G. longifolia. This means that as populations age beyond about 15 years post-fire, annual seed output (and the amount of seed successfully reaching the soil seedbank) will decline in G. caleyi at a much greater rate than in G. longifolia. The soil seedbank

-in G. caleyi is small and declines to low levels some 20 years after fire. In G. long\$olia, the soil seedbank, although limited in magnitude by mammal seed predation, is more persistent through time. This suggests that G. longifolia will better tolerate long unburnt periods that G. caleyi. Comparable data is not available for G. shiressii.

-In Sydney, heat from a fire does not break seed dormancy in Grevillea species, although a post-fire flush of seedlings is evident (Auld and Tozer 1995, Table 1). Hence, the amount of fuel consumed in a fire may have no effect on post-fire germination levels. Such germination should be governed by the response of seeds to another fire-related germination cue as well as the rate of decay of dormant seeds to a non dormant state in the soil seedbank. Leachates from charred **wood** (Keeley 1991), smoke (Brown 1993, Dixon et al. 1995) and nitrate and ammonium ions (Thanos and Rundel 1995) have all been shown to be fire-related cues that break seed dormancy
-{6}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
-**Figure 3.** Fecundity **after** fire in Grevillea. a) **G.** caleyi; *and b) G. longifolia.*
-in fire-prone habitats. Which cues are critical in *Grevillea*  species in Sydney remains to be investigated.

-The key management indicators for healthy populations of *G. caleyi* in long unburnt (>15-20 year old) areas would appear to be the levels of adult survival and mammal seed predation. Such areas now occur as very small isolated pockets within urban areas. At sites where survival is low and mammals **are** destroying most of the seeds produced in any one year, seeds in the soil will continue to persist, but the magnitude of the soil seedbank will decline and the population is likely to be reduced after the next fire. This suggests that consideration should be given to burning such sites before the seedbank declines too much. Any such burning should be of a large spatial extent to reduce the densities of mammalian seed predators after fire.
-# **Implications for Fire Management**

-What are the implications for the management of these obligate seeding species? The most critical aspect of fire management for obligate seeders is the impact of frequent fires on these populations. Population declines or local extinctions are predicted after 2-3 fires occurring in close succession and hence, minimum fire-free intervals are needed to maintain the species. The fire free-intervals will vary depending on the rate of replenishment of the soil seedbank after any one fire and the proportion of seeds that emerge from the seedbank after a fire (ie, the degree to which the seedbank is depleted after a fire). Estimates of the minimum fire free intervals needed to maintain populations of threatened *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species vary from **5-** 10 to 8-12 years (Table 2). It is not only important to maintain these threatened species, but also the species with which they CO-habit. These suggested minimum fire-free intervals do not contradict with suggested minimum fire-free intervals for other plants species that CO-habit with threatened *Danvinia* and *Grevillea*  species (Bradstock and Auld 1987). Consequently, for the long-term survival of threatened species of *Darwinia*  and *Grevillea* and their associated vegetation communities, under a regime of repeated fires, care should be taken to accurately record the fire histories of all remaining populations. This will allow sites potentially threatened by high fire frequency to be identified.

-In *Darwinia* species, where heat is the fire-related cue that breaks seed dormancy, some residual seedbank should be present after any single fire. The amount and location of this seed will depend on the level of soil heating during the passage of a fire (Bradstock and Auld 1995). In *Grevillea,* the fire-related dormancy breaking cue is unknown, although it is not simply heat (Auld and Tozer 1995). In *Grevillea,* a high proportion of seeds within the soil seedbank may emerge after any one fire and in some
